questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Distance Between Two Parallel Axes
questions.problem:
A circular plate of mass $1\,\text{kg}$ with uniform mass density occupies the region of a disk $D$ of radius $\sqrt{6}\,\text{m}$ and is centered at the origin.
Given that the moment of inertia of the plate about a line $l$ perpendicular to the plate is $4\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2},$ find the distance of the line $l$ from the center of mass of $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

First, notice that the region $D$ can be expressed in polar coordinates as

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le \sqrt{6},\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

The area of the circular plate $D$ is $A=\pi \cdot (\sqrt{6})^{2}=6\pi \,{\text{m}}^{2}.$
Since the plate has a uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{1}{6\pi }\,\text{kg}/{\text{m}}^{2},
$$

and its center of mass is its centroid $(0,0).$

Then, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{6\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{6}}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{6\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}\,{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{6}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{6\pi }\cdot 9\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =3\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem and solving for $d,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\ 4 & =3+1{d}^{2} \\ {d}^{2} & =1 \\ d & =1\,\text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Moment of Inertia of a Rectangular Plate About a Perpendicular Axis
questions.problem:
A rectangular plate of mass $6\,\text{kg}$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,\,-3\le y\le 3},$
where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about a line perpendicular to $D$ at a distance of $\sqrt{3}\,\text{m}$ from a parallel line passing through its center of mass.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=4\cdot 6=24\,{\text{m}}^{2}.$
Since the plate has a uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{6}{24}=\frac{1}{4}\,\text{kg}/{\text{m}}^{2},
$$

and its center of mass is its centroid:

$$
(\overset{¯}{x},\overset{¯}{y})=(\frac{-2+2}{2},\frac{-3+3}{2})=(0,0)
$$

Since the center of mass is at the origin, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}{\int }_{-3}^{3}\frac{1}{4}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-2}^{2}{[{x}^{2}y+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{y=-3}^{y=3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-2}^{2}6{x}^{2}+18\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[2{x}^{3}+18x]_{-2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(32+72) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(104) \\  & =26\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a line $\sqrt{3}\,\text{m}$ from the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\  & =26+(\sqrt{3})^{2}\cdot 6 \\  & =26+18 \\  & =44\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Distance Between Two Parallel Axes
questions.problem:
A rectangular plate occupies the region
$D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 6,\,0\le y\le 4}$
and has mass density function $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{1}{8}x,$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters. The moment of inertia of the plate about a line $l$ perpendicular to the plate is $39\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$
Given that the center of mass of the plate is at $(4,2),$ find the distance of the line $l$ from the center of mass.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

First, we find the mass of the plate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{8}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{0}^{6}x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{4}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\,{|}_{0}^{6}\cdot y\,{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot 18\cdot 4 \\  & =9\,\text{kg}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass $(4,2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}((x-\overset{―}{x})^{2}+(y-\overset{―}{y})^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}((x-4)^{2}+(y-2)^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}{\int }_{0}^{4}((x-4)^{2}+(y-2)^{2})\cdot \frac{1}{8}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{0}^{6}{\int }_{0}^{4}x(x-4)^{2}+x(y-2)^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{0}^{6}{[x(x-4)^{2}y+\frac{1}{3}x(y-2)^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{0}^{6}4x(x-4)^{2}+\frac{16}{3}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{0}^{6}4{x}^{3}-32{x}^{2}+\frac{208}{3}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{[{x}^{4}-\frac{32}{3}{x}^{3}+\frac{104}{3}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(1\,296-2\,304+1\,248) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot 240 \\  & =30\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem and solving for $d,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\ 39 & =30+9{d}^{2} \\ 9{d}^{2} & =9 \\ {d}^{2} & =1 \\ d & =1\,\text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Moment of Inertia of a Rectangular Plate About a Perpendicular Axis
questions.problem:
A rectangular plate occupies the region
$D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 3}$
and has mass density function $\lambda (x,y)=xy,$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters.
Given that the center of mass is at $(\frac{2}{3},2),$ find the moment of inertia about a line perpendicular to $D$ at a distance of $1\,\text{m}$ from a parallel line passing through its center of mass.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

First, we find the mass of the plate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{3}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{|}_{0}^{1}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass $(\frac{2}{3},2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}((x-\overset{¯}{x})^{2}+(y-\overset{¯}{y})^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}+{(y-2)}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}({(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}+{(y-2)}^{2})xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}x{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}y+x{y}^{3}-4x{y}^{2}+4xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}x{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{4}-\frac{4}{3}x{y}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{9}{2}x{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}+\frac{81}{4}x-36x+18x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{9}{2}x{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}+\frac{9}{4}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{9}{2}{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}+\frac{17}{4}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{9}{8}{x}^{4}-2{x}^{3}+\frac{17}{8}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{9}{8}-2+\frac{17}{8}-0 \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a line $1\,\text{m}$ from the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\  & =\frac{5}{4}+{(1)}^{2}\cdot \frac{9}{4} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}+\frac{9}{4} \\  & =\frac{7}{2}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Moment of Inertia About a Perpendicular Axis Using Polar Coordinates
questions.problem: Calculate the moment of inertia of a circular plate that occupies the region of an annulus $D$ centered at $O$ with inner radius $1\,\text{m},$ outer radius $4\,\text{m},$ and mass density $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{|xy|}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}},$ measured in $\text{kg}/{\text{m}}^{2},$ about a line perpendicular to the ring passing through a point $1\,\text{m}$ from its center.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

First, notice that the region $D$ can be expressed in polar coordinates as

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 4,\,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

Since the mass density is symmetric in $x$ and $y,$ the center of mass is at $(0,0).$ The mass density function, in polar coordinates, is given by 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{|r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta |}{r}=\frac{1}{2}r|\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )|.
$$

Next, we find the mass of the plate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{2}r|\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )|\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}|\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )|\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{r}^{3}{|}_{1}^{4}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(64-1)\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =21\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =42\,\text{kg}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{2}r|\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )|\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}|\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )|\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}{|}_{1}^{4}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(1024-1)\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1023}{5}\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{2046}{5}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a line $1\,\text{m}$ from the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\  & =\frac{2046}{5}+{1}^{2}\cdot 42 \\  & =\frac{2046}{5}+\frac{210}{5} \\  & =\frac{2256}{5}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
